lessons.title: What a Tax Regime Is and Why India Has Two

children.text: Priya joins Infosys in Bengaluru on a ₹10 lakh package. Before her first payslip, the HR portal asks one question: Old Regime or New Regime? She clicks whatever looks default and moves on. That single click decides how much tax leaves her salary every month. Most first-time taxpayers treat it as a form field. By the end of this lesson, you will treat it as a decision.

body.text: A tax regime is not a scheme you invest in. It is a rulebook for calculating your tax. India gives you two rulebooks for the same income, and you are allowed to pick the one that costs you less.

children.text: What a Tax Regime Actually Is

markDefs.definition: A complete set of rules for computing income tax: the slab rates, the rebate, and which exemptions and deductions you are allowed to claim.
An income band taxed at a fixed rate. Only the portion of income that falls inside a band is taxed at that band's rate.
Income that is excluded from your taxable salary in the first place, such as House Rent Allowance within prescribed limits.
An amount subtracted from your gross total income because you spent or invested it in a way the law rewards, such as PPF, ELSS or health insurance premiums.

children.text: Every income tax calculation answers two questions. First, how much of your income is taxable? Second, at what rates is it taxed? A
is the package of answers. It fixes the
rates, the rebate, and the list of
you may claim. Change the regime and both answers change, even though your salary stays exactly the same.

body.caption: The same formula runs in both regimes. The regime decides what goes into each bracket. The 1.04 is the 4% Health and Education Cess (surcharge for high earners is covered in Chapter 3).

columns.label: Old Tax Regime
points: Higher slab rates: 20% starts above ₹5 lakh, 30% above ₹10 lakh
Rewards specific behaviour: PPF, ELSS, life insurance, health insurance, home loans, paying rent
Standard deduction of ₹50,000 for salaried employees
Rebate makes tax nil only up to ₹5 lakh of taxable income
More paperwork: rent receipts, investment proofs, loan certificates

columns.label: New Tax Regime
points: Lower, wider slabs: 30% applies only above ₹24 lakh
Most deductions and exemptions are removed
Standard deduction of ₹75,000 for salaried employees
Rebate makes tax nil up to ₹12 lakh of taxable income
Almost no proofs to submit, and it is the default

body.title: Quick Check: What Changes Between Regimes?
body.question: Rohan earns the same ₹14 lakh salary whichever regime he picks. What actually changes when he switches from the old regime to the new regime?
options: His gross salary and his employer's CTC
The slab rates applied and the deductions he is allowed to claim
Only the 4% cess, which is waived in the new regime
Nothing, both regimes always produce the same tax
body.explanation: A regime never changes what you earn. It changes the rules applied to that income: which slab rates, which rebate, and which exemptions and deductions are allowed. The 4% cess applies in both regimes.

children.text: How India Ended Up With Two Rulebooks

For decades, India ran one system with fairly high rates and a long menu of tax breaks. The breaks were meant to push savings into PPF, insurance and housing. Over time the menu grew so long that tax planning became a February scramble for proofs, and many breaks helped mostly those with the surplus cash to use them. The government's answer was not to abolish the old system overnight. It built a second, simpler one next to it.

events.title: One regime, many deductions
events.description: The Income-tax Act, 1961 builds up a large set of exemptions and deductions, from Section 80C investments to HRA and home loan interest.

events.title: The new regime is born as an option
events.description: Section 115BAC introduces lower slab rates for individuals willing to give up most deductions, effective from FY 2020-21. Few salaried taxpayers switch at first.

events.title: New regime becomes the default
events.description: From FY 2023-24, the new regime applies unless you opt out. The ₹50,000 standard deduction is extended to it and the rebate limit rises to ₹7 lakh.

events.title: Standard deduction raised
events.description: The new regime's standard deduction goes up to ₹75,000 and its slabs are widened. The old regime is left unchanged.

events.title: Nil tax up to ₹12 lakh
events.description: New regime slabs are restructured and the rebate is raised so that taxable income up to ₹12 lakh pays no tax. For a salaried employee that means ₹12.75 lakh of salary after the standard deduction.

events.title: Income-tax Act, 2025 takes effect
events.description: The 1961 Act is replaced. Both regimes carry over, section numbers change, and 'previous year' and 'assessment year' merge into a single 'tax year'. Tax year 2026-27 is the first under the new law.

body.text: Why not simply scrap the old regime? Millions of people signed up for 20-year home loans, 15-year PPF accounts and long-term insurance policies on the promise of tax breaks. Removing those breaks overnight would have broken that promise. Keeping the old regime as an opt-out option lets those taxpayers stay put while everyone else moves to lower rates.

children.text: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the new regime sits in Section 202 (Section 115BAC of the 1961 Act) and the rebate sits in Section 156 (Section 87A). You will still see the old numbers on many payslips, investment declarations and blog posts, so this course shows both.

body.title: New Law, New Term
body.textWithBlank: From 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single term: the ___.
body.explanation: Under the 1961 Act, income earned in FY 2025-26 was assessed in AY 2026-27, which confused almost everyone. The 2025 Act uses one label, the tax year, for the year you earn the income and pay tax on it.

children.text: The whole course comes down to one trade: lower rates in the new regime versus deductions in the old one. Here is Priya's ₹10 lakh salary run through both rulebooks in two versions, first with no tax-saving at all, then with a heavy set of deductions.

New regime: taxable income ₹9,25,000. Slab tax is 0 on the first ₹4 lakh, 5% of ₹4 lakh (₹20,000) and 10% of ₹1,25,000 (₹12,500), total ₹32,500. Taxable income is below ₹12 lakh, so the rebate wipes out the full ₹32,500. Tax: ₹0.

Old regime, no deductions: taxable income ₹9,50,000. Slab tax is 0 on the first ₹2.5 lakh, 5% of ₹2.5 lakh (₹12,500) and 20% of ₹4,50,000 (₹90,000), total ₹1,02,500. No rebate, because income is above ₹5 lakh. Add 4% cess of ₹4,100. Tax: ₹1,06,600.

Old regime, with deductions: ₹1,50,000 under Section 80C, ₹25,000 health insurance under Section 80D, ₹1,20,000 HRA exemption and ₹50,000 extra NPS contribution, total ₹3,45,000. Taxable income ₹6,05,000. Slab tax is ₹12,500 plus 20% of ₹1,05,000 (₹21,000), total ₹33,500. Add 4% cess of ₹1,340. Tax: ₹34,840.

body.text: Notice what happened. Even after claiming ₹3.45 lakh of deductions, Priya pays ₹34,840 more in the old regime. At her income level the new regime's rebate is so large that deductions cannot catch up. That flips at higher salaries, which is exactly what Chapter 3 teaches you to test.

body.title: Your Turn: Old Regime Tax
body.prompt: Arjun's taxable income under the old regime, after all deductions, is ₹7,00,000. Calculate his total tax including 4% cess. (Old regime slabs: 0 up to ₹2.5 lakh, 5% from ₹2.5 lakh to ₹5 lakh, 20% from ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh.)
body.explanation: 5% of ₹2,50,000 is ₹12,500. 20% of the next ₹2,00,000 is ₹40,000. Slab tax is ₹52,500. No rebate, because taxable income is above ₹5 lakh. Cess at 4% is ₹2,100. Total: ₹54,600.

body.title: Priya's Flatmate at the HR Portal
body.scenario: Karthik, 23, joins a Pune startup on a ₹7,20,000 salary. He pays ₹12,000 a month as PG rent, has no investments, no insurance and no loans. His HR portal wants a regime declaration by Friday.
body.prompt: Without doing a full calculation, which regime should Karthik lean towards, and why?
body.modelAnswer: New regime. His salary minus the ₹75,000 standard deduction is ₹6,45,000, well below the ₹12 lakh rebate limit, so his tax is nil. For the old regime to also reach nil, his taxable income would have to fall to ₹5 lakh. After the ₹50,000 standard deduction he would still need ₹1,70,000 of HRA exemption and deductions, and he has no investments at all. There is nothing to gain from the old regime and more paperwork to do.

body.text: The choice you make on your employer's portal only decides how much TDS is cut from your salary during the year. If you have no business or professional income, you can still pick either regime when you file your return. Chapter 4 covers the switching rules in full.

cards.definition: A complete rulebook for computing tax: slab rates, rebate, and allowed exemptions and deductions.
The new regime. It applies automatically unless you actively opt for the old one.
Income kept out of taxable salary from the start, such as eligible HRA. Mostly unavailable in the new regime.
An amount subtracted from gross total income for eligible spending or investing, such as Section 80C or 80D.
A reduction in the tax itself for lower incomes. Makes tax nil up to ₹12 lakh (new) or ₹5 lakh (old) of taxable income.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 term that replaces both previous year and assessment year.

body.title: Before You Answer Your HR Portal
steps: Download your CTC breakup and note your basic salary and HRA components
List what you already invest each year: EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums
Note your monthly rent and whether you have rent receipts or a rent agreement
Check for a home loan interest certificate or health insurance premium receipts
Find your employer's regime declaration deadline for this tax year

body.label: Income Tax Department Tax Calculator
body.description: The official e-filing portal calculator lets you compare your tax under both regimes. Keep it open as you work through this course.

points: A tax regime is a rulebook for computing tax, not an investment product. Your salary stays the same in both.
The old regime pairs higher slab rates with a long list of deductions and exemptions. The new regime pairs lower slab rates with almost none.
The new regime became the default from FY 2023-24. You must actively opt out to use the old one.
In tax year 2026-27, the new regime's rebate makes taxable income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free, against ₹5 lakh in the old regime.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 carries both regimes forward under new section numbers: Section 202 (115BAC) and Section 156 (87A).
Whichever regime is cheaper depends on your income and how much you can genuinely claim, which is what the rest of this course teaches you to test.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Figures reflect the rules applicable to tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing. Tax rates and limits can change in every Union Budget, so confirm against the latest Finance Act or a qualified tax professional before filing.
